A novel approach is developed to calculate the eikonal quasinormal modes using the matching conditions in the near-horizon and asymptotic regions, where the quasinormal modes are found to be significantly affected by the higher-order corrections. The shadow observed in the near-horizon region is then analyzed and the modifications caused by the higher-order corrections are studied. A comprehensive examination of the shadow's properties such as defocusing, staticity, and extremality is performed.

The Pulsar Timing Array acts as a highly sensitive tool for identifying and analyzing low-frequency gravitational waves through the investigation of inter-pulsar correlations. The traditional approach of examining direct correlations has been supplemented by the "common-band" method, which involves applying Fourier filter design techniques to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio of the gravitational wave signal. In this paper, we demonstrate that the traditional analysis can be interpreted as applying a filter and subsequently applying a least-squares estimation on the resulting data. The paper then explores the optimal filter settings that yield the highest signal-to-noise ratio for the gravitational wave signal. However, we find that the filter's optimal performance is compromised by the presence of noise, which necessitates the use of regularization techniques to mitigate this issue. The regularization methods employed in this study are comparable to those used in common-band processing and are found to be effective in reducing noise in the traditional analysis as well.

This study proposes a set of necessary and sufficient conditions for the support constrained generator of MDS codes, presented in two forms: one to guarantee and the other to verify. These criteria stem from a combinatorial analysis of Walsh matrices and their generalizations, the GHW matrices. To verify these results, the necessary background on the properties of GHW matrices is introduced, including a proof of their symmetry, orthogonality, and relation to Hadamard matrices. An efficient algorithm is developed to check the verification conditions, running much faster than the necessary conditions, when applied to specific instances of GHW matrices.

We define a class of generalized truncated Toeplitz operators, known as unbounded truncated Toeplitz operators, which have matrix-valued symbols that are limited to a specific range. We prove that these operators meet the criteria for being equivalent to their rank-one counterparts, a property also shared by traditional truncated Toeplitz operators. Furthermore, a corresponding concept of a kernel function is established, which is proven to be well-defined and yields the correct generalized Toeplitz operator when applied.

In a Bayesian context, we investigate the influence of individual trials within a sequence of diverse experiments. To accomplish this, we utilize a modified version of the classic scoring function developed by Cramer, which assigns greater significance to more significant trials. The resultant influence function exhibits desirable properties, including finite influence and the ability to generate well-defined posterior distributions even in the presence of infinite sample spaces. Moreover, this influence function is adaptable to various Bayesian model selection scenarios, and it is shown to produce the expected posterior probability of a particular hypothesis over another hypothesis (Kullback-Leibler distance) in the limit of large sample sizes.

This paper introduces a novel method for automatically detecting anomalies in multichannel audio signals without the need for labeled data. The proposed approach relies on the manifold technique UMAP for creating a visual representation of audio signal embeddings and pinpointing anomalies. To enhance the model's resilience against domain-shifts, we implement self-attention for audio feature extraction and incorporate adversarial training into the embedding layer. We also utilize the UMAP representation to perform one-class classification and validate our approach using publicly available datasets.

In the context of $N$-component ultra-cold fermionic atoms, we investigate the ground state of fermions with attractive interactions, when the interaction strength is at a critical point where bound state formation is possible. Due to the presence of multiple body interactions, the ground state wave function exhibits non-trivial, complex fluctuations, characterized by a non-local order parameter. These fluctuations are reminiscent of nomadic ferromagnetism, a phenomenon studied extensively in the theory of magnetism, in which magnetic moments are randomly aligned and interact with other dipoles at a distance. The nature of these fluctuations is influenced by the number of fermions involved, and we explore the occurrence of such behavior in various configurations, including small groups of fermions and larger clusters. Furthermore, we analyze the behavior of these configurations in the thermodynamic limit, and their potential presence in a sparse gas of fermions.

Our research involved a stacking analysis of gamma-ray pulsars to uncover potential signs of dark matter annihilations or decays using data from Fermi. We explored mass ranges from 10 keV to 100 TeV and examined annihilation and decay rates for all standard channels. After conducting a thorough search, our investigation did not yield any statistically significant evidence for dark matter signals. As a result, we established upper limits on cross-sections or decay rates within specific annihilation or decay channels. These findings can be interpreted as limits on the mass-dependent annihilation cross-section or the decay length, providing a comprehensive assessment of dark matter properties.

In this research, a comprehensive theoretical framework is developed to analyze the impact of an external magnetic field on the quantum Hall systems of electrons and holes within two-dimensional space, with a focus on the effects of spin-orbit interactions and electron-hole mass differences. Our findings reveal that varying the magnetic field strength results in distinct "magnetotron series," each with unique low-energy excitations characterized by specific spin-parity rules. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of the low-energy excitations reveals that an external magnetic field introduces a distinct set of spin-parity rules for each exciton in the system. Utilizing the developed theory, we provide detailed predictions for the behavior of magnetotrontons and magnetothresholds in quantum Hall systems, with a focus on the specific examples of electron-hole excitons in GaAs/AlGaAs and excitons in WSe$_2$/MoSe$_2$ semiconducting heterostructures.

The Intense Energy Occurrences experiment, known as IEO, is a cutting-edge research project utilizing the Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics's 10 MeV electron linac. The primary goal of this project is to investigate the phenomenon of intense laser-matter interaction. The following discussion highlights IEO's successful operation and achievement in terms of telescope performance.

The Cauchy problem for the truncated Boltzmann equation is studied under minimal initial data conditions. By developing a highly efficient, high-dimensional particle method and a novel, low-cost collision resolution strategy, significant gains in computational performance are achieved. The proposed approach enables the control of Cauchy problems with low initial density values and long-range interactions, facilitated by a novel, low-cost collision resolution method. The proposed method also exhibits improved computational scalability, allowing for increased spatial and temporal resolution without increasing computational costs.

Machine learning models are susceptible to compromised training data, often intentionally altered or maliciously modified for adversarial purposes. This can occur when labels are intentionally changed or contaminated during data collection. Consequently, it is crucial to develop machine learning classifiers that can effectively operate on noisy datasets, even with incorrect labels. This study introduces a new evaluation metric called the clean-to-noise ratio, measuring a model's ability to maintain accuracy on clean data while tolerating corrupted labels within a dataset. Furthermore, our analysis involves assessing the effectiveness of robust learners on datasets with noisy labels, utilizing the MNIST dataset as a reference point.

This study delves into the automorphism groups of a specific class of cyclic orbit codes, which exhibit simplified generator matrices due to their defined structural properties. The researchers develop a method to calculate the automorphism groups for these codes, allowing them to create automorphism groups for specific classes of cyclic orbit codes, including those derived from average codes and orbit average codes. The study further explores the existence of automorphism groups exhibiting particular properties, including being cyclic or containing a cyclic subgroup, and develops corresponding necessary and sufficient conditions for their existence. The researchers apply these findings to classify the existing automorphism groups for particular cases, including those of prime-power length codes, resulting in a complete classification of the different automorphism groups for a specific class of maximal cyclic orbit codes.

A binary star system within the open cluster M67, featuring a turnoff multiple system, has been identified and analyzed. The primary star in this system has a mass of 1.43 solar masses, while the companion star has a mass of 0.79 solar masses. By utilizing the cluster's age and metallicity, both derived from eclipsing binary measurements, a precise mass-radius relationship for the primary star was established. The resulting values were then compared to theoretical models, showing that the observed radius of 1.63 solar radii is larger than predicted by models, indicating significant stellar evolution. Furthermore, this study's results suggest that the cluster's age is 4.0 billion years, with a margin of error of 0.2 billion years. The findings also indicate that the cluster's metallicity is similar to that of the Sun, with an error margin of 0.05 times the Sun's value. The observed stellar radius inflation is believed to be caused by external factors, such as stellar wind, rather than internal processes, including those related to stellar rotation.

We investigate the Sturm-Liouville operator $\mathscr{L}_c = -d^2/dx^2+cx^\alpha$ for $\alpha \neq -2, -1,$ and its associated eigenvalues and eigenfunctions on the half-line $[0, \infty)$ to determine the most sufficient condition for which the spectral type changes from discrete to continuous.

A revised SPH formulation is presented, addressing two key SPH issues: the reproducibility of the gradient field and the accuracy of density conservation. By leveraging a partition of unity approach, our method minimizes the need for extra penalty forces and momentum transfers, significantly improving gradient field reconstruction. This enables the use of a simplified, density-conserving equation that is independent of the smoothing radius and not influenced by the gradient estimation method. The accuracy of our approach is demonstrated through a variety of test cases, including the modeling of a spherical drop under surface tension or the inflation of a balloon.

The primary objective of spectral super-enhancement is to extract the original spectral image from a mixed image containing information from multiple spectral bands. This task is crucial in various applications such as remote sensing and hyperspectral imaging. However, it is challenging due to the significant differences in intensity and content among images from distinct spectral bands. To address this issue, a novel method called the pixel-sensitive deep function-blend network (PS-DFN) has been developed. This method combines the strengths of dense pixel information and global contextual information to achieve better results. It consists of a two-stage framework where the first stage utilizes a pixel-sensitive network to predict the original spectral image, while the second stage leverages a function-blend module to refine the prediction based on the differences between the predicted and target spectral images. Experimental results on three datasets demonstrate that the proposed PS-DFN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

In this study, we introduce an object geotagging approach that relies on the context of an object's location, rather than its visual features alone. By training a deep learning model to predict an object's presence at a given location based on its surrounding context, rather than specific object characteristics, we can effectively identify objects in unfamiliar environments. Our approach yields superior results compared to traditional methods that focus solely on object appearance. Notably, we achieve an accuracy of 83.2% on a real-world dataset containing diverse object categories and a wide range of environmental contexts.

The removal of dams in natural rivers has become a global priority, leading to efforts to dismantle structures built across rivers worldwide. This removal is crucial for restoring natural river processes and mitigating the ecological damage inflicted by existing dams. A significant hurdle in achieving dam removal lies in assessing the remaining reservoir volume, as it poses a safety risk and is a complex task that requires specialized equipment. To address this challenge, our research proposes a machine learning-based approach that utilizes high-resolution satellite images to estimate the reservoir volume of dams before and after their removal. We developed a tailored metric for this purpose and tested it using images from the Google Earth Engine library, demonstrating its effectiveness in accurately predicting the reservoir volume with an average relative error of 8.3%.

Quantum Field Theory and Superstring theory share a significant connection 
between them, and both are built upon the concept of space-time. In classical 
physics, space-time is a straightforward concept, but in quantum theory, it's a 
complex idea. Understanding the relationship between Quantum Field Theory and 
Superstring theory involves understanding how space-time behaves at the quantum 
level. This paper delves into the concept of the QFS-zone and its impact on 
space-time.

E-commerce shoppers often struggle to pinpoint the exact product category for a product they're interested in, so we propose a system that utilizes text and image data to forecast the point-of-attraction category before the product is added to cart. This system is informed by the fact that shoppers typically view product listings in categories matching their desired item. We've developed a multi-modal deep learning model that combines text and image features to make predictions, and our approach outperforms traditional baselines and a single-modal text model in a prominent e-commerce setting.

Our research examines the connection between shareholder confidence as indicated
by annual earnings call Q&A responses and subsequent share price variations. We
develop a quantitative method to measure investor sentiment by analyzing these dialogues.
Our case study on an Indian company demonstrates that anticipated future performance
significantly influences share price movements, outperforming traditional forecasting
methods in some instances.

This paper investigates the problem of optimally placing wireless sensors in a multi-level network, with the goal of maximizing coverage of a 3D area with diverse points of interest. The research considers a uniform distribution of sensors and a fixed communication radius, with the area to be covered divided into uniform 3D pyramids above diverse locations. The paper presents a new optimization approach that uses a combination of linear programming and integer programming techniques to find the optimal sensor placement, with the goal of minimizing the number of sensors required to achieve full coverage. The research also develops a new algorithm that uses a combination of dynamic programming and integer programming to find the optimal sensor placement, with the goal of minimizing the number of sensors required to achieve full coverage.

A novel quantum algorithm has been developed to identify entangled quantum eigenstates within polynomial time, utilizing a quantum eigenstate selection algorithm. This method employs a hybrid approach that combines quantum and classical computations to achieve an efficient solution. The algorithm has been proven to identify an entangled eigenstate with a high degree of probability, given a known lower bound on the absolute value of an eigenvalue. The algorithm's effectiveness has been demonstrated for application in resolving quantum linear systems. The algorithm has been shown to outperform existing methods, particularly for large matrices and positive definite systems, where it can achieve a significant speedup, resolving a previously open problem in a time complexity that scales quadratically.

We examine the behavior of compact gauged infant skyrmions within a non-linear environment. By analyzing a model that incorporates a $\mathsf{\mathfrak{SU}(2)}$ gauge field and a nonlinear sigma field, we discovered a novel gauged infant skyrmion solution. Our findings indicate the presence of a single stable gauged infant skyrmion solution, which is defined by the governing parameters and the distance from the center of the skyrmion. Furthermore, we investigated the energy profiles of the model, which revealed that the internal energy of the gauged infant skyrmion is a function of the radius and asymptotically approaches the energy of a topological $\mathsf{\mathfrak{SU}(2)}$ skyrmion. Additionally, we derived the first-order corrections to the energy of the skyrmion in the low-energy limit and determined the decay length of the correction fields.

This study explores the potential for novel interactions at the Standard Model, focusing on four new operators - $Q_{W\phi}$, $Q_{ZW}$, $Q_{WW}$, and $Q_{W\phi H}$ - which encompass W-boson anomalous dimensions and interactions between Higgs bosons and $Z$-bosons. The research utilizes data from the LHC at 13 TeV, its upgraded level, and the proposed FCCee collider at 80 TeV, to derive and analyze the corresponding Wilson coefficients. The study also evaluates the sensitivity of current and future experiments to these operators, finding that the future experiments exhibit significantly higher sensitivity than the current data. The research further investigates the potential for obtaining information on these operators through the production of Higgs bosons in association with $W$-boson pairs at the LHC and FCCee, and the sensitivity of the latter to these operators, revealing comparable sensitivity to existing measurements of the Higgs self-coupling.

A diamond nuclear rotor cryogenic clock was successfully developed and showcased at the Temva 2021 exhibition in Berlin, achieving a remarkable precision of one second over 10,000 years. This innovative timepiece features a 5-teardrop diamond with a total weight of approximately 0.4 carats, which was acquired through a partnership between De Grisogono and the CERN.

The development of whole-cell models has accelerated significantly over the past few years, driven by advancements in computational power, experimental data, and sophisticated modeling techniques. In this article, we provide an overview of the latest progress in whole-cell modeling, including the methodologies used to build and analyze these models and the resulting benefits for biological research. We also discuss the challenges that must be addressed before whole-cell models can be widely accepted in the scientific community.

This paper introduces a novel mobile Multi-View Object Visual Search (MOVS) system designed to efficiently search for three-dimensional objects in a real-world environment. The system's architecture is composed of three key components: a multi-camera network, a cloud-based server, and a mobile client. The multi-camera network captures and processes visual data from various viewpoints, which is then stored in a database and utilized by the mobile client for query refinement. The mobile client generates query features and predicts object locations, which are transmitted to the cloud server. The cloud server leverages a query-object matching algorithm to predict object locations and confidence scores, which are then relayed back to the mobile client. Experimental results demonstrate the system's effectiveness in improving search accuracy and reducing localization errors on a real-world dataset.

A promising approach to seizure detection is Hyperdimensional (HD) computing, 
which offers a unique, efficient, and robust framework for identifying seizures 
from EEG signals. Although HD computing has shown potential, its performance can be 
improved by refining its underlying methods. This study delves into the effects of 
two key HD computing strategies: the number of samples used to create hypercodes and 
the threshold for determining similarity between them. By employing a more efficient 
methodology that balances learning complexity with prediction accuracy, we have found 
that a smaller dataset yields superior results. Furthermore, by relaxing the criterion 
for similarity between hypercodes, we have found that a more relaxed threshold leads 
to improved performance. Notably, the optimal settings for these parameters vary 
depending on the specific dataset being used. This study contributes to the 
development of a more effective HD computing framework for seizure detection.

Future advancements in gravitational wave technology will allow for precise measurements of the Hubble constant, Hubble-Standard-Siren (H-SS) observation, by utilizing binary black hole mergers. We investigated the potential of Deci-hertz gravitational wave observatories to contribute valuable insights into the universe's cosmological properties. Our research focused on a network of ground-based and space-based observatories, modeling their sensitivity to binary black hole mergers across varying mass ranges. We simulated the detection of these sources over multiple cosmic epochs, incorporating different redshift distributions, and then analyzed the precision with which their measurements would constrain the Hubble parameter. Our findings suggest that even relatively low-frequency gravitational wave observatories can provide significant information about the Hubble parameter, especially when combined in a network configuration.

We introduce QALD-9-Plus, an enhanced version of the QALD-9 benchmark, which incorporates additional data and a more comprehensive description. The task of answering questions through knowledge extracted from databases has been a key focus in question-answering research, particularly within the Open Domain question-answering area. The QALD challenge has played a significant role in driving progress in this area. The QALD-9-Plus dataset builds upon the QALD-9 benchmark by retaining its existing question types and adding new ones, thereby expanding its scope. The addition of new questions is achieved by translating the existing ones into French, German, Italian, Spanish, and Chinese, and then re-annotating the translated questions with new answers sourced from DBpedia and Wikidata. The QALD-9-Plus dataset is designed to facilitate the evaluation of question-answering systems that utilize various knowledge sources and languages, thereby enabling researchers to assess their systems' performance across different question types and languages.

The machine learning community has been actively exploring various resampling methods to efficiently extract and describe insights from datasets, particularly through the use of resampling techniques such as permutation tests and bootstrapping. However, these methods have several drawbacks, including the need for multiple iterations and the inability to directly compare insights. In response, we propose a new approach that combines resampling with a renaming mechanism to effectively summarize insights and compare the importance of different features across various datasets. Our method, known as the Hindsight Summarizer, utilizes a decision tree to build a naming system for the features in a dataset, with each branch representing a distinct subset of the dataset. This approach allows for the direct comparison of the relationships between subsets of the data, providing a comprehensive understanding of the underlying structure. In our experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the Hindsight Summarizer in uncovering new insights in both simulated and real-world datasets, including the discovery of correlations that were not previously known.

As AI-powered medical diagnostics gain traction, it's crucial to address the issue of bias in these systems, which can lead to incorrect or unfair outcomes. Detecting inherent bias in data sets is vital to prevent such issues. In medical imaging, where AI models are widely used, data sets are typically annotated by medical professionals, who may unintentionally introduce biases due to their own perspectives and the characteristics of the data. To tackle this problem, we've developed a method for detecting bias in medical image data sets, leveraging the principles of adversarial learning. Our approach aims to minimize the differences in image representation when demographic attributes are ignored, and these differences are maximized when those attributes are taken into account. We've tested our method on various medical imaging data sets, including chest X-rays, skin lesions, and mammograms, and compared it to existing bias detection methods, which share the same input and output structure. Our results show that our model outperforms these methods, achieving higher accuracy and better recall.

This paper tackles the issue of noisy labels in metric learning caused by the high dimensionality of the embedding space. To achieve robust metric learning, we introduce a novel loss function called Prox-Angle Loss. This function uses proxy-based learning to estimate the angle between the embedding and its corresponding label, while accounting for noisy labels by estimating the angle between the embedding and its contaminated label. To further mitigate the impact of noisy labels, we propose a new loss called Sleek Proxy-Anchor Loss, which uses the distance between the embedding and its contaminated label to estimate the angle, thus reducing the influence of noisy labels. This loss is shown to be more effective than existing methods in metric learning tasks.

The 3D correlation function of galaxies is used to measure the distribution of matter on large scales, but it is affected by the complex structure of galaxies. A new measure, the 3D Density Gradient Adjusted Correlation Function (dDACF), is presented as a solution to overcome these limitations. This measure, based on the 3D correlation function, is less susceptible to the complexities of galaxy structure and can be applied to future surveys. A comparison with the 2D correlation function shows that it can be used to obtain similar results, but with greater accuracy in certain conditions. A new measure, the density gradient exponent, is introduced to quantify the impact of galaxy structure on the correlation function, showing a correlation with the density of galaxies. This study highlights the importance of accounting for galaxy structure in the analysis of large-scale structures.

A theoretical framework for understanding topological superconductivity has been developed, which builds upon the concept of a topological insulator in 2D. This framework involves a 2D system with fermions that are confined to different energy levels, which interact with each other in a way that preserves time reversal symmetry. The interactions within this system can be described using a specific mathematical formalism, which reveals that certain patterns of interaction can give rise to unique types of quasiparticles. These quasiparticles can exist in a variety of forms, including Majorana quasiparticles and Majorana-2 quasiparticles, which have been observed in certain superconducting systems. The framework also allows for the prediction of other types of quasiparticles, including certain types of fermionic quasiparticles. To demonstrate the validity of this framework, a 2D model of a superconducting system was developed, which exhibits the predicted types of quasiparticles. The results of this model provide a concrete example of how the principles of topological superconductivity can be applied to real-world systems.

A prototype of a multi-anode photodetector has been created and its performance in detecting avalanche has been assessed. The developed device exhibits a high number of sensitive areas, with over 200 detection points, each consisting of a reverse-biased junction coupled with an optically activated gain structure. The optically stimulated avalanche process is analyzed by registering the signals from individual detection points within the device, each connected to a dedicated electronic channel. The device's capabilities are demonstrated through its ability to identify specific events, such as single-photon responses, resulting from the detection of a light pulse with a low energy threshold of 10^-4 photons. The device's multi-point detection areas enable the identification of avalanche processes initiated in semiconductor materials with low impact ionization coefficients. The device's multi-point detection areas enable the identification of avalanche processes initiated in semiconductor materials with low impact ionization coefficients.

We establish connections between a Coxeter group's partial generalized Deligne $l$-valued invariants and the Cohen-Macaulay ring associated to its parabolic Bruhat graph, specifically how this index relates to the ring's Krull dimension when considering a particular partial genus.

A specific type of Aurivillius material called bismuth titanoferrate, Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$, when compressed into a solid state, shows a significant change in its magnetic properties. By using a technique called nuclear forward scattering, researchers were able to study the material's behavior under high pressure and temperature, and discovered that the change in magnetic properties is due to the material's reduced size and altered crystal structure. Furthermore, the team found that the change in magnetic properties is reversible, and that the material's magnetic properties are significantly influenced by the high pressure, resulting in a solid state that is similar to the material's melting point at room temperature.

A fund advisor's daily activities incur substantial costs, primarily due to brokerage fees, tax liabilities, and fund size constraints. These expenses have a profound impact on investment outcomes. To address this, we've developed a comprehensive framework for assessing and ranking brokerages based on their estimated net costs. Our approach involves a two-part methodology: first, we utilize a novel algorithmic trading evaluation method that accurately calculates net costs by accounting for both transaction costs and fund size limitations. Subsequently, we employ a Bayesian hierarchical model to analyze a sample of large institutional investors' portfolio strategies to estimate the underlying cost components. By combining these estimates, we provide a comprehensive picture of net costs associated with various brokerages.

We've developed a novel add-drop device combining optical and mechanical components. By incorporating a single optomechanical cavity with two optical resonators, our design enables the manipulation of optical add-drop operation through precise control of a mechanical parameter. The cavity's optical modes are connected via a frequency conversion mechanism, and we've identified conditions for achieving a completely adjustable add-drop configuration. Our findings also reveal that the optical frequency conversion plays a crucial role in this flexibility, as it allows the manipulation of optical add-drop parameters.

The internet has become an essential resource for understanding how various groups interact within their communities. By analyzing online content, such as social media and forums, we can uncover the dynamics of interest between different communities and the ways in which they influence one another. This study focuses on the impact of online sports discussions on local community engagement in the United States, as measured by the number of people participating in volunteer work for local non-profit organizations. To this end, we have compiled a large database of online sports discussions and identified relevant topics of interest, such as professional and amateur sports, which we then matched to specific U.S. cities. By examining the relationship between online sports participation and local volunteer work, we found a significant connection between the two, as well as notable variations in the intensity of this connection across different cities.

Image lossless compression can be achieved using predictive image compression, which involves predicting image areas and encoding the remaining errors. This method is comparable to JPEG in quality and outperforms it in compression ratio, with significant potential for real-time applications due to its suitability for GPU processing. However, current approaches are hindered by the use of complex, non-CPU-friendly prediction and encoding methods. To address this limitation, we introduce PILC, a GPU-oriented neural architecture for predictive image lossless compression, aiming to strike a balance between quality, compression ratio, and real-time processing capabilities. PILC employs a convolutional neural network-based prediction scheme and a probabilistic neural encoder, which can be fully trained on a single GPU in under 200 hours. Our experimental results demonstrate PILC's effectiveness on the Urban100 dataset, showcasing its competitive performance relative to JPEG2000 and state-of-the-art image predictors.

The LHCb experiment detected the $B^{+}$ to $D_s^{+}K^{+}K^{-}$ decay with a significant level of confidence at a $6.8\sigma$ threshold, collecting a large amount of $4.9$ or $5.0$ femtobarns of collision data. The experiment was able to determine the branching ratio of this decay as $f_{B^{+}\to D_s^{+}K^{+}K^{-}} = 7.1 \pm 0.5 \pm 0.8 \times 10^{-6}~K^{0}_{S}$. Additionally, the experiment was able to determine the branching ratio of the $B^{+}$ to $D_s^{+}K^{+}K^{-}$ decay relative to the $B^{+}$ to $D_s^{+}K^{-}K^{+}$ decay as $R(D_s/K) = 1.27 \pm 0.15$. Furthermore, the experiment was able to determine the $D_s^{+}$ decay width by combining the $B^{+}$ to $D_s^{+}K^{+}K^{-}$ and $B^{+} to D_s^{+}K^{-}K^{+}$ decay branching ratios with the $B^{+}$ to D^{0}K^{+}K^{-}$ decay branching ratio. The data processing methods of optimal transport and its variants rely on the assumption that data distribution probabilities remain constant over time. However, this assumption is violated in many real-world scenarios where data distribution probabilities change over time due to factors such as data loss, bias, and uncertainty. To address this issue, we introduce a novel concept called anomaly-robust ideal transport that aims to minimize the impact of changing probability measures on optimal transport solutions. We formulate this problem as a linear optimization of transport plans and derive a solution using a dual approach, which we demonstrate and compare to existing robust optimization methods through numerical experiments.

In order to fully realize the potential of artificial intelligence, it is essential to develop AI agents that can effectively collaborate with humans. Currently available AI models are either overly simplistic, relying on basic decision-making strategies, or overly complex, employing machine learning approaches that are difficult for humans to understand and work with. To address this challenge, we propose a novel hybrid model that combines the strengths of human and machine learning. Specifically, we use machine learning to simulate human decision-making patterns and then employ reinforcement learning to train agents to collaborate with humans in a way that is both efficient and understandable. Our approach was tested in a complex scenario, where a human and artificial agent work together to resolve a series of puzzles. The results demonstrate that our hybrid model not only outperforms a purely machine learning approach but also does so while maintaining a high degree of transparency and human-centered cooperation.

A theoretical framework is proposed to enhance the reliability of the supersymmetry spectrum.  The model is based on a modified version of the supersymmetric standard model, where the number of gaugino doublets is maximized to eight, and the number of Higgs doublets is minimized to one.  The model is characterized by a large number of superpartners, and their masses are influenced by a single scaling parameter.  The model is designed to be more accurate than the supersymmetric standard model, and the superpartners' masses are coupled to the scaling parameter.  The model is also invariant under a new type of symmetry, the supersymmetric scaling symmetry, and the superpartners' masses are scaled by the scaling parameter.  The model is also found to be stable and long-lived, and the superpartners' masses are scaled by the scaling parameter to achieve this property.  The model is also found to be predictive, and the superpartners' masses are scaled by the scaling parameter to achieve this property.

To assess the impact of domain-specific expertise on visualization task performance, we conducted a study involving 160 participants in three disciplines - data analysis, geography, and architecture. Our goal was to determine if professionals and students within these fields, as well as novice participants, exhibited the same levels of accuracy and speed when completing non-numerical tasks on visualizations. Our results indicate that, in contrast to tasks requiring numerical input, skills related to task performance are largely influenced by the type of domain expertise individuals possess, rather than their level of educational attainment.

We introduce a novel loop construct, known as the clause set loop, utilizing the concept of quasi-models to expedite the induction proof search. Specifically, the loop iteratively refines a quasi-model by applying induction axioms to generate quasi-models that satisfy these axioms. Our approach has been successfully integrated into the Isabelle/HOL logic platform, and preliminary results reveal that it not only boosts the performance of inductive proof search but also enhances the overall system's performance.

We propose a novel approach to graph extraction referred to as Aligning Models for
Graph Extraction, or AMGE. This method is distinct from the conventional
approach of aligning observations to existing graphs, instead aligning observations
to generate new underlying graphs that best reflect the data provided. AMGE
enables flexible underlying structures and learns the relationship between the
data and the graph, allowing it to be applied across a wide range of domains,
including structured data, text, and images. We demonstrate the effectiveness
of AMGE using a variety of real-world datasets and showcase its ability to learn
complex relationships between structured data and underlying graphs that
capture meaningful patterns.

Deep learning models have excelled in language processing tasks, but their training methods have a notable limitation - they primarily focus on static predictions rather than capturing dynamic behaviors. In contrast, the field of physics and machine learning has seen success with physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in solving partial differential equations (PDEs), yet these approaches often struggle with complex, high-dimensional problems. To address this, we introduce a novel training framework that combines the techniques of language models with the architecture of PINNs, leading to the development of a more efficient and robust PINN method. Our approach, which we call neural language models (NLMs), is comprised of a new training strategy and architecture that incorporates language motivated techniques, including a combination of supervised and self-supervised learning, and a hierarchical structure that enables the simulation of transient phenomena. We demonstrate the effectiveness of NLMs through experiments on a range of challenging problems, including the Navier-Stokes, heat, and wave equations, in high-dimensional spaces.

This research introduces a novel approach to dividing resources among agents in a fair and efficient manner. A new algorithm has been developed to achieve optimal results in a specific class of resource distribution problems. The method relies on a mathematical framework that enables the creation of a fair division plan given a single-peaked preference ranking among agents. The algorithm either produces a fair allocation that meets certain criteria or demonstrates that no such allocation is possible. Additionally, the approach includes a mechanism for enforcing compliance, where a specific allocation is chosen and agents are incentivized to select it. Furthermore, the method enables the determination of whether a specific allocation meets certain criteria or not, allowing the development of a specific type of voting mechanism that is resistant to manipulation.

The task of coreference resolution is crucial in numerous natural language processing applications, particularly when it comes to processing news articles. However, most existing methods are geared towards standard texts and may not perform optimally on news-specific content. News articles frequently feature entities that are mentioned before and after by other entities, making the identification of these 'occurrence coreferences' essential. To address this, we've developed a two-stage approach that first identifies occurrence coreferences and subsequently resolves the remaining coreferences. The system is evaluated using a dataset derived from news articles covering political controversies.

This paper introduces a new set of polyhedral facets for the complementarity knapsack problem, a problem that has gained significant attention in recent years due to its numerous real-world applications. The problem is characterized by interrelated lower and upper bound constraints that require special consideration. Building on previous research, we have expanded the existing facets by incorporating additional ones, including perfect and strong facets, thereby enhancing the linear programming relaxation's accuracy and computational efficiency in solving the original problem, ultimately leading to potential reductions in solution times.
This paper defines and explores the properties of generalized $(m,n)$-Jordan derivations and centralizers for semiprime rings.

We derive Weinberg's 2-parameter tensor solely from the constraints imposed by the helicity properties of the one-loop amplitudes in $n$ external lines. Specifically, a set of four helicity states corresponds to a specific scattering configuration known as the "double crossing configuration", where Weinberg's 2-parameter tensor is the only remaining mass dimension-one tensor that fulfills the requirements of gauge invariance. By applying this to $n$-gluon one-loop integrals, we are able to extract the 2-parameter tensor from the remaining independent terms after expanding the numerator. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Weinberg's 2-parameter tensor can be reconstructed from the $n-4$ amplitudes with $0++,++,---,$ and $--++$ helicity configurations, and we provide an explicit expression for this reconstruction.

We explore the properties of a specific class of groups, known as the transversal group of a submixture within a mixture M, where M encompasses all nonlinear transformations between finite-dimensional vector spaces. This investigation reveals connections between the transversal group and a nonlinear equivalent of the Favard length, which was previously defined for a particular linear operator. This research also extends to examining the transversal group of a specific type of nonlinear operator, the Jacobian operator, in addition to introducing a new measure for quantifying the complexity of a mixture M.

This study introduces a novel, efficient approach to finding the optimal policy for complex systems using model-based methods. The algorithm, called Resilient Tube Direct Policy Search, uses a previously developed tube MPC method that maintains system stability under various disturbances. Building on this concept, the researchers created a policy network by replicating the tube MPC algorithm, allowing them to leverage its robustness. The resulting policy network serves as an initial guess for a simulated annealing algorithm, significantly reducing the computational time required to find the optimal policy compared to traditional methods. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm, showing that it outperforms existing approaches by a factor of 80 times in terms of computational efficiency.

The discovery of topological phases has been a major breakthrough in condensed matter physics, and a key phenomenon, the anomalous Hall effect, is a direct result of this. This effect arises from the Berry curvature, a vector field in momentum space that arises from the Berry connection. This paper proposes a new approach to calculate the Berry curvature, enabling the prediction of a previously unobserved third-order anomalous Hall phenomenon. According to the findings, the third-order anomalous Hall conductance is zero in two-dimensional systems but can exist in three-dimensional systems under specific conditions. This result is attributed to the unique properties of the Berry curvature, which exhibits a certain symmetry in momentum space.

This paper introduces an innovative method for compactly representing a team of call graphs with a single unified representation that captures the essence of all the graphs. Our approach involves merging individual call graphs into a unified graph and then simplifying it into a condensed form using a specific data structure. We have developed an algorithm that optimizes the merging process by strategically selecting the most relevant edges to include, allowing the resulting graph to be efficiently processed and analyzed by existing tools. We have tested our method using a large dataset of 1,685 call graphs from the SZZ revision set and generated a single unified call graph that is 0.2% the size of the original collection.

A widely used text dataset has been driving the development of natural language processing models for over a decade, but we question whether it offers the benefits its proponents claim, given its impact on model size and the resulting models' limited generalizability. We examine the history behind the benchmark, its influence on natural language processing, and the effects of training on large models, before proposing a simple method to create a more effective benchmark. Our analysis reveals that the current benchmark's limitations stem from its narrow scope and the characteristics of the texts it contains, rather than any inherent flaws. We demonstrate that the same corpus can produce models with even better results when a more targeted approach is employed.

The formation of quasi-periodic oscillations in flare coronal loops is often linked to the dynamic instability in the flare current sheet. To investigate this connection, we simulated the dynamics of a flare current sheet in a three-dimensional model, incorporating the resistive tearing instability and its effects on a cusp-shaped sheet. The model revealed that the formation of quasi-periodic oscillations is primarily driven by tearing mode instability, which in turn is influenced by resistivity, magnetic field strength, and density. The results also showed that the oscillations, which occur at frequencies of a few hundred Hz, can be detected in microwave and X-ray emissions, offering a new approach to studying flare dynamics.

A novel multi-scale framework for anomaly detection in industrial quality evaluation is introduced, and its application to a diverse range of real-world datasets is showcased. Traditional quality evaluation methods typically rely on manual data inspection due to the complexity of identifying anomalies within high-dimensional datasets. To address this challenge, most current approaches employ unsupervised anomaly detection algorithms that often fail to capture the nuanced relationships between different variables. To overcome these limitations, a multi-scale framework is proposed, combining the strengths of several state-of-the-art anomaly detection methods. By leveraging these techniques, a comprehensive understanding of anomalies can be achieved, enabling the accurate classification of instances based on their normal or anomalous status. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to six diverse real-world datasets, where it has achieved impressive performance, outperforming existing algorithms in all six cases.

We examine a modified version of the KP-I equation, which includes a dispersion term and has a certain level of non-linearity. This model is well-behaved in terms of regularity, with only a minimal level of irreducible behavior. In a fixed time context, our study demonstrates that small scale data with negative regularity, subject to certain constraints, can flow into the initial conditions at a finite time scale, a phenomenon that is a direct result of dispersion. The conditions that govern this phenomenon are based on the interaction between negative and positive regularity, a concept that is a direct result of dispersion. This model is a unique example of how negative regularity can lead to the breakdown of certain properties. In a separate analysis, we have also shown that small scale data with negative regularity, subject to certain constraints, can cause the model to become ill-conditioned.

The Kramers' degeneracy of degenerate ground states in spin-polarized ferromagnetic materials is broken by thermal fluctuations due to the Heisenberg exchange interaction, but can be restored through the thermalization of higher excited states. This phenomenon is studied in an open quantum system framework, where the system interacts with its environment to allow for non-unitary time evolution. By using a stochastic Liouville-von Neumann equation, the time-dependent quantum distribution function is calculated to show the reversal of Kramers' degeneracy increase in certain excited states. The results are validated by comparing them with exact numerical calculations for a simple spin model.

In highly-mobile MIMO networks, predicting future channel state information (CSI) responses is essential to optimize handover processes between base stations. Our research focuses on developing a predictive model that forecasts CSI responses from nearby base stations, leveraging the user's current location, the user's velocity, and past measurements. Our proposed model, based on long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, effectively predicts CSI responses, particularly channel delay and Doppler spreads, by first extracting relevant features from the input data. Our results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves high prediction accuracy, particularly when compared to linear regression and LSTM approaches, thereby providing a reliable solution for predicting future CSI in highly-mobile networks.

In stereo matching, accurately determining regions with minor disparities is a significant challenge. Current methods often rely on optimization procedures that can be computationally costly. To overcome this issue, we suggest an alternative approach that identifies minor region areas based on a mixture model consisting of two components: a beta distribution and a mixture of two beta distributions. The parameters of the proposed model components are estimated using the Expectation-Maximization algorithm. Furthermore, we incorporate our model into the stereo matching process and present a customized cost function that integrates the model's disparity metric. Experimental results validate the efficacy of our proposed method.

We investigate the spectral measures of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on a Grauert cylinder, which is the unit cotangent bundle of a compact Riemannian manifold. In doing so, we derive scaling limits for the Szegö kernels on these manifolds, and prove a Grauert cylinder analogue of a theorem initially proposed by B. Shiffman, E. Verchota, and G. Weinstein.

In 2008, Lee and Lee hypothesized that the category of rigid modules over a one-dimensional algebraic variety X over an algebraically closed field is equivalent to the category of coherent sheaves on X that are twisted by a vector bundle. We have successfully proven this hypothesis specifically for non-isolated singularities, utilizing results from van den Bergh's work on the non-commutative projective line.

To maintain quality and ensure software security, it's crucial to have a precise understanding of software dependencies. Overestimating dependencies, however, can lead to unnecessary effort in incorporating new libraries, delayed adoption of critical security fixes, and decreased visibility to potential security threats. Although previous research has identified inaccurate dependency declarations, there is a lack of information regarding the prevalence of inaccurate declarations and the evolution of these inaccuracies over time. This study investigates the accuracy of Java dependency declarations and tracks its changes over a 12-year period, utilizing a dataset comprising 1,000 randomly selected open-source projects. Our analysis of 1,000 projects revealed a significant issue of inflated dependencies, with an average of 14% of declared dependencies being inaccurately declared, while studying the impact of these inaccuracies over time revealed a notable decline in their prevalence, from 34.2% in 2009 to 14.2% in 2019.

This research focuses on the biphoton regulated synthesis (BRS) model, specifically the relationships between hostilities and relations within its graph structure. The study identifies a core-injecting hostilities, a key graph component, and explores its properties, while also establishing that BRS forms are connected through their core-injecting hostilities, forming a complete graph. The research further demonstrates the applicability of these findings to other graph structures, including the Harary graph, and shows that BRS generates a core-injecting hostilities matrix.

We address multistage distributionally robust optimization problems involving uncertainty, adopting a risk measure that combines a conditional value-at-risk objective with robust constraints, subject to an adversary's power constraint. This adversary can manipulate distributions through a power set of scenario-based distributions, with the power parameter indicating the adversary's influence. We develop a scenario-based algorithm for a specific instance of these problems involving a linear objective, an Lp norm constraint, and a robust constraint, and analyze its performance. We derive a condition under which the algorithm's performance approximates that of the theoretical optimum, expressed in terms of the adversary's power parameter. We further extend our approach to a broader class of robust optimization problems involving nonlinear objectives.

Predicting actions based on a video's frames is a complex task, especially when it comes to anticipating future frames. Most existing approaches rely on a causal relationship between frames and, therefore, are not well-suited for predicting future frames. In an effort to improve upon this limitation, we propose a new method that employs a non-causal strategy for frame prediction. By utilizing a video's future frames to forecast future actions, our approach can achieve better results. To accomplish this, we developed a Feature Mapping LSTM model, which incorporates a feature mapping layer with a Radial Basis Function (RBF) activation. The Feature Mapping LSTM learns to map video frames to a latent space, where it uses temporal dependencies to generate predictions. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through experiments on two action prediction datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance on these benchmarks.

We investigate an approach to resolving the fundamental thermalization process of the 1D discrete nonlinear Schrödinger equation by introducing a novel class of solvable initial conditions. These conditions are characterized by a unique combination of pre-thermalization, thermalization, and post-thermalization phases, which are marked by distinct spectral properties of the Floquet operator. Specifically, the initial condition exhibits a unique spectral gap during the pre-thermalization phase, closes at the thermalization point, and reappears at the thermalization plateau. These spectral properties are directly related to the emergence of solvable integrable channels. Our study demonstrates that the thermalization process is significantly influenced by the initial condition's solvable integrable properties. Moreover, we introduce a new concept of "thermalization times" based on the spectral gap properties and demonstrate that the system reaches thermalization in a finite time frame. These findings provide a framework for understanding the interplay between integrability and thermalization in quantum many-body systems.

This article delves into the examination of boundedness and nuclearity of 
pseudo-differential operators within the framework of functions defined over 
uniform trees. A key finding presented in this paper involves establishing a 
relationship between boundedness of certain pseudo-differential operators and 
Bessel potentials in tree-structured spaces, which mirrors a corresponding result 
in Euclidean settings. Additionally, we prove that a subset of these operators 
possesses the property of being microsupported, thereby rendering them both 
bounded and compact. Furthermore, we investigate the nuclearity characteristic of 
pseudo-differential operators, demonstrating that a substantial category of these 
operators can be shown to be both bounded and nuclear.

The widespread adoption of 5G technology has led to a significant expansion of cellular networks, now covering a vast array of diverse environments, including both urban and rural settings. This expansion has created numerous opportunities for potential threats to emerge, including malicious entities that exploit unsecured areas. A new study examines the unique visibility of 5G networks in various locations, highlighting the crucial role of cellular antennas and the impact of smartphone models on signal detection in different frequency bands. The research reveals that some smartphone models, such as the Samsung Galaxy S10, can detect cellular signals more effectively across a wider range of frequencies and in diverse environments, including both urban and rural settings. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that these smartphone models can detect cellular signals in areas where other devices fail to do so, including in rural settings, even when using the same antenna. The researchers also found that the frequency range of these smartphone models has a significant impact on signal detection, with some frequencies being more effective than others in detecting signals in rural areas. These findings have significant implications for the security of 5G networks and their potential vulnerability to threats.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) often overestimate their accuracy on out-of-distribution (OOD) images, leading to inaccurate predictions. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a novel approach called CODEs that identifies OOD instances based on their geometric properties. By analyzing the results of two distance metrics - the Chamfer distance and kernel maximum mean discrepancy - we observe that OOD images exhibit unique characteristics. Specifically, CODEs identifies OOD instances as those with high similarity to multiple class images but low similarity to each other. By combining these features, we achieve superior performance compared to existing methods in detecting OOD instances on popular datasets.

The CDF and CMS collaborations initially discovered a correlation between the angles of jets in e$^+$e$^-$ collisions containing heavy quarks as intermediate particles. This study investigates similar connections within proton-proton collisions measured by CMS. Results were obtained for up to 4-jet events at a 13 TeV center-of-mass energy, with a focus on angular correlations between the first two jets. These outcomes were compared to self-correlations of simulated multijet events generated by PYTHIA 8 and corrected by TAUOLA for $\mathrm{\mathrm{K}}^0_\mathrm{\mathrm{S}}\mathrm{\mathrm{\pi}}^+$ decays.

Deep learning has been instrumental in achieving outstanding visual analysis outcomes. However, the high cost of annotating data has hindered the development of deep learning models. This limitation has led to the emergence of semi-supervised and unsupervised deep learning techniques, which have gained significant attention in recent years. These methods, which utilize unlabeled data, have been employed to improve visual education outcomes. This research aims to provide a comprehensive overview of semi-supervised and unsupervised deep learning techniques, including their applications in visual education. A novel taxonomy is proposed to categorize existing methods, and a thorough analysis is conducted to compare their performance. The findings of this research will serve as a valuable resource for researchers, enabling them to select suitable techniques for tackling visual education challenges.

In many real-world applications, sensor data often contains inaccuracies due to malfunctions, changes in environment, or calibration issues. Identifying and correcting these anomalies is crucial for data reliability. We introduce RECol, a novel method for flagging anomalous sensor data by leveraging the performance of a predictive model trained on clean data. Unlike existing approaches that rely on statistical methods or machine learning outputs, RECol examines the differences between actual sensor readings and reconstructed values based on future readings. These discrepancies can indicate anomalies. We validate the effectiveness of RECol on a range of data sets, including a large-scale dataset from a university's smart building monitoring system, showing its capability to accurately identify anomalies.

This research focuses on a specific type of mathematical model, the non-linear Young equation, which describes a particular kind of fluid flow. By breaking down this equation into simpler forms using certain mathematical theorems, researchers can study its behavior under different conditions. One such method, known as the Lyapunov theorem, can be applied to determine the long-term behavior of this model. Another approach, the existence theorem, can be used to study the behavior of this model in different conditions. By combining these methods, researchers can better understand the behavior of this model and make predictions about its behavior under different conditions. The utility of this model was demonstrated through an example, which showed that it can be used to study the behavior of fluid flows under various conditions.

The possibility of non-zero neutrino mass causing a difference in neutrino and antineutrino behavior is investigated. This difference can be attributed to the neutrino polarizability having distinct values for neutrinos and antineutrinos. An updated analysis of the astrophysical implications of this phenomenon is performed using a combination of theoretical models and observational data. This analysis yields a lower limit on the difference in neutrino polarizability, indicating that $\Delta \mathcal{P} \gtrsim 1.5 \times 10^{-18}$ cm$^2$.

In a model of the neuron-glial network, incorporating both neurons and astrocytes, we investigate the dynamic behavior of the system, particularly when considering the rhythmic activity of the astrocytes.  We examine the model's mean field representation, identifying a set of parameters for which the system exhibits oscillatory behavior.  We then analyze the long-term evolution of the system's states, demonstrating that a unique solution exists and exists solely when the parameter values lie within a specific range.  Furthermore, we demonstrate that the oscillatory behavior of the model is a result of the system's bistability, resulting from the interaction between the astrocytes and either the neurons or themselves.  Our findings suggest that the ability of the astrocytes to regulate their own activity, through the consumption and regulation of excess glucose, plays a critical role in the system's behavior, resulting in the emergence of rhythmic activity.

We investigate the behavior of a neutral particle with half-spin in a magnetic field that varies geographically, combining the principles of quantum optics and topological physics. Our research reveals that this system possesses unique topological characteristics, including a Berry phase that cannot be found in other known systems. By studying the energy levels of the particle, we can observe the emergence of topological resonances that form at specific points within the energy spectrum. Additionally, we can derive a specific mathematical model that describes these topological resonances, which can be observed in the energy spectrum as a result of the particle's behavior under certain conditions.

We've developed a novel method for eroding a boundary in a two-dimensional flow field by incorporating vortical structures that emerge during initial flow transitions. This approach is efficient and controllable, allowing for precise control over the rate of boundary erosion at any point. Our method has been successfully applied to a variety of flow scenarios, including both time-independent and evolving flows. Notably, we've found that boundary erosion can occur even in cases where the initial flow pattern is stable, and that this effect can persist for an extended period without the need for continuous input. Our method has potential applications in engineering contexts, such as the removal of oceanic boundaries for offshore platform installation, and it could also be used to model natural processes such as coastal erosion.

We've developed a method to create a hyperbolic knot's complete invariants by combining the formal semigroup generated by its knot group with a specific set of operations. This approach allows us to identify a subset of L-space knots and determine whether certain knots, known as (n,m)-torus knots, are L-space or not. Additionally, we've developed a new tool to analyze an infinite algebraic structure, the free profinite semigroup, and applied it to analyze an even more complex structure, the free profinite monoid, in the context of knot theory.

We introduce a kinetic theory for a system of interacting particles that leads to a Poisson equation for hydrodynamics, even when entropy is not uniformly distributed. This approach is based on the idea that the mean field is represented by the local entropy level. Our method allows for a direct derivation of the Poisson equation, eliminating the need for a double iteration process. Our findings are applicable to both thermal equilibrium and non-equilibrium regimes. We have successfully applied this approach to a system of ideal gas particles interacting via the Vlasov-Poisson equation and obtained a novel Poisson equation that takes into account non-uniform entropy levels. Our numerical simulations confirm the accuracy of this new equation.

The use of machine learning-based object detection in analyzing endoscopic video footage has been explored in the context of identifying surgical tools. This study compares the performance of three widely used object detection models, SSD, YOLOv3, and FPN, when applied to a dataset of endoscopic images. A novel approach is also presented, which combines the predictions of these detectors to improve resilience and efficiency. The goal is to enable reliable real-time monitoring of surgical toolkits during procedures. A collection of 10,000 images of various surgical instruments was annotated and used to train and evaluate the performance of these models. Results show that FPN outperformed SSD and YOLOv3 in terms of mean average precision, achieving an average of 0.8508, 0.8269, and 0.7951, respectively. The approach that combined detector outputs yielded an average precision of 0.8709, surpassing the individual performances. A collection of 10,000 annotated images is proposed to facilitate the development of robust surgical tool detection systems.

A common practice in programming, giving expressive and meaningful names to variables and functions, is crucial in code understanding. Research has shown that developers use syntax to create patterns in the code names, which can be crucial in code comprehension. This work delves into the creation and meaning behind these syntax-based patterns in source code names. A study of 10,000 Java methods from Open Source projects found that these patterns are widespread and essential for code understanding. Our analysis tool, SynLex, was used to identify these patterns and discovered that they are created by developers to convey meaningful information about the code, such as method purpose, type, and semantic relationships. Furthermore, our results show that these patterns can be used to predict the presence of certain code properties, which can be useful in code analysis.

We create a novel infinite-dimensional $\square_q$-structure that originates from the $q$-shuffle algebra associated with the affine $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Lie algebra. This construction is achieved by utilizing the infinite-dimensional affine $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ and the $q$-difference operators based on the $q$-Hecke algebras. We also demonstrate that the $q$-difference operators satisfy the $\square_q$-relation, and in addition, derive an infinite-dimensional realization of the $q$-deformed Heisenberg-Virasoro algebra. This construction is found to generalize previous results for infinite-dimensional $\square_q$-structures derived from the affine $A_1$ Lie algebra.

The evolution of grain structures in polycrystalline materials is a complex process influenced by factors such as initial grain size, number of grains, and time. Understanding the dynamics of grain growth in materials with multiple grains is crucial for developing stronger and more efficient materials. This study uses a mathematical model to investigate the effects of different grain numbers on grain growth in materials with varying initial conditions. The research reveals that as the number of grains increases, the rate of grain expansion slows down, leading to a slower rate of grain development. Interestingly, the number of grains has a more significant impact on grain growth than the initial conditions. The findings suggest that as the number of grains increases, the rate of grain development increases more rapidly, leading to a slower rate of growth at higher grain numbers. The initial conditions, on the other hand, have a less significant impact on grain growth, with a more significant effect observed at lower grain numbers. The results also indicate that as the number of grains increases, the rate of grain development increases more rapidly, leading to a slower rate of growth at higher grain numbers. The study provides new insights into the kinetics of grain growth in materials with multiple grains, with implications for the development of stronger and more efficient materials.

Human pose estimation is a fundamental challenge in computer vision, with a significant body of research focused on 3D pose estimation. This work presents a comprehensive analysis of existing 3D human stance and form assessment techniques, highlighting their advantages and limitations. A novel dataset, referred to as HSSD, is introduced, comprising images of humans in diverse settings, varying lighting conditions, and poses. The dataset is annotated with ground truth labels for key aspects such as center of mass, neck, and joint locations, as well as body part orientations and pose estimations. The results of the initial experiments on HSSD are presented, which demonstrate the dataset's capacity to expose existing technique limitations, ultimately facilitating a thorough evaluation of state-of-the-art techniques.

In this study, we explore the phenomenon of superconductivity in a two-dimensional lattice with a sparse arrangement of available energy levels, characterized by a significant electron-electron repulsive force and a single unfilled energy level at each site. Utilizing the renormalization group method, we investigate the phase transition from a Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer state to a Fulde-Ferrel-Larkin-Ovchinnikov phase as the interaction strength increases. Our analysis reveals that, in certain interaction regimes, the transition to the superconducting state is facilitated by a fluctuation-driven mechanism, where the interaction strength is sufficiently low.

The standard model Higgs boson interactions with fermions are generated by the coupling with scalar leptoquarks.  We establish constraints on the scalar leptoquarks' vacuum expectation value based on the requirement of electroweak vacuum stability.  The stability of scalar leptoquarks is also evaluated in the context of the minimal extension of the standard model. The concept of categories is a fundamental element in various branches of science and mathematics, particularly in the realm of dynamical systems. In machine learning and artificial intelligence, category theory has played a pivotal role in ensuring the integrity and consistency of algorithms. Despite its significance, this subject remains largely underrepresented in mainstream academic literature. In an effort to bridge this gap, this article delves into the core principles of category theory and its practical applications in machine learning, offering a unique perspective through the lens of cognitive linguistics.

This paper addresses the robust closed-loop tracking issue for dynamic systems prone to disturbances and uncertainties, utilizing a sliding-mode control approach. A novel technique is presented, providing an analytical framework for designing a optimal boundary control law capable of achieving final endpoint convergence in the presence of disturbances and uncertainties, utilizing a single time-varying surface with adjustable parameters. The control law is defined in terms of system states, disturbances, and uncertainties, with parameters adjusted via a gradient-based algorithm. The method is validated through simulation-based testing.

To enhance the performance of lithium-ion batteries, it's crucial to comprehend how external factors such as vibrations affect their internal structure and dynamics during charging and discharging. This study investigates the impact of applied ultrasonic vibrations on Li-ion batteries, focusing on how it disrupts the solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) and alters the layer arrangements within the electrodes. By employing a novel approach that combines electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and ultrasonic vibrations, we demonstrate that the treatment causes a re-arrangement of the layers within the electrodes, leading to an improvement in battery performance. Utilizing a previously developed model, we quantify the electrode layer configuration before and after ultrasonic treatment, revealing a significant reduction in average layer resistivity. This reduction in resistivity, measured to be 1.8 ohm cm, translates to a notable increase in battery capacity, up to 20%.

This research introduces a discrete-time controller for a gantry hoist based on an level-level controller formulation, expanding the traditional continuous-time version. Discrete versions of the equations often lead to unstable and unreliable Gantry Hoists. To address this issue, a novel discrete-time controller is proposed for the levelled system, capable of controlling the position of the load. This solution is compared to a traditional continuous-time controller and shown to be more robust and efficient in discrete-time settings.

Recent large-scale datasets of image-caption pairs have led to significant advancements in image description technologies. However, these systems are only as good as their data and can be vulnerable to weaknesses inherent in the data, such as poor quality captions. To address this, we've developed a novel approach called collaborative distillation that enables image description models to learn from multiple models at once, thereby filtering out low-quality data and improving overall performance. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach not only withstands noisy data but also boosts model capacity and robustness, ultimately resulting in enhanced image description capabilities as evident from our top rankings on the Vizwiz and localizating referring expression understanding subtasks.

We define a collection of finite word sequences as strongly interconnected if the partial words formed by combining any two of these words aren't equal, with the goal of categorizing all strongly interconnected sets of sequences. A strongly interconnected set is either fully composed of primitive words or possesses a specific, simplified form that we've identified, in which case we've determined that the size of such a set is at most six. Our findings also include a broader, structural analysis that enables us to organize all strongly interconnected sets of sequences into distinct categories.

This study develops a category of monoids that adhere to a specific geometric framework and classifies a key subcategory within it. An instance of this theory is the monoid of arrangements on a set, which focuses on sequences of elements, and it exhibits a natural isomorphism to a semigroup of partial one-to-one mappings. Furthermore, this study explores the characteristics of monoids within this category and it provides a detailed categorization of monoids in this category that have a specific property.

However, we demonstrate that the effectiveness of self-focus is not solely dependent on the number of layers, but also on the interaction between layer depth and width. We found that widening a self-focused network significantly enhances its performance, and this effect is more pronounced when the number of layers is greater than a certain threshold. We also discovered that the optimal number of layers for self-focus and the ideal width are inversively proportional, and that the ideal width for a given depth is directly related to the number of layers.
